newsitem.title: CONGO: Brazzaville sends troops to fetch Rwandan refugees.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville sends troops to fetch Rwandan refugees.

text.p: The Congolese government in Brazzaville has sent barges protected by troops up the Congo River to try to assemble Rwandan war refugees crossing from the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo, aid workers said on Thursday.
A former military training ground at Bilolo north of Brazzaville has been prepared for temporary accommodation of the Hutu refugees, displaced by recent fighting in the former Zaire.
Aid workers estimate more than 8,000 refugees crossed, fleeing the advance of Laurent Kabila's forces who took Kinshasa on Saturday after a seven-month sweep across the vast country.
Some 120 Rwandan refugees who fled Kinshasa at the weekend and were camping out at Red Cross headquarters in Brazzaville were transferred by minibus to Bilolo on Tuesday, a Red Cross spokesman said.
They will soon be joined by a much larger group clustered around the town of Liranga, 400 km (250 miles) north of Brazzaville on the Congo River.

Boris Michel, a spokesman for the International Committee of the Red Cross, said he had received as yet unconfirmed reports that as many as 15,000 refugees could be grouped around Mbandaka, in Kabila's Congo opposite the river from Liranga, with the aim of crossing into Congo.

A convoy of barges left Brazzaville on Saturday to collect refugees from sites upriver as far north as Liranga. They are expected to arrive back in Kintele, 50 km (30 miles) north of Brazzaville by the middle of next week. After a couple of days' rest in Kintele the refugees will be transferred to Bilolo.
As many as 5,000 are expected to board the barges manned by teams from the Red Cross and the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR and protected by Congolese troops.
They are transporting high-protein biscuits and plastic sheeting. The barges arrived in Makotipoko, midway between Brazzaville and Liranga, on Tuesday, the Red Cross said.
The government, which is not commenting on its plans for the refugees, is thought to have retained the Bilolo site to keep the refugees close to Brazzaville airport and speed their repatriation.
The camp was last used to house about 1,000 Tutsi refugees who fled Kinshasa last November.
Kabila's war to topple Zaire's dictator Mobutu Sese Seko started as a revolt by ethnic Tutsis over citizenship. Tutsis were quickly hounded out of Kinshasa.

The refugees crossing this time are mostly Rwandan Hutus, among them former soldiers and hardliners accused of massacring up to 800,000 minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994 before fleeing to Zaire. They now fear revenge both from Kabila's Tutsi-led forces and the Tutsi-dominated army back in their homeland.
Aid workers said Congo wanted to avoid the term "refugees" altogether and to refer to "displaced persons in transit".
"They're obviously very worried about Laurent Kabila," said an expatriate aid worker.
The huge presence of refugees on Congolese soil is unlikely to go down well with Kabila, whose spokesmen have warned neighbouring states against admitting armed Hutus.
"Even when they've been disarmed you can still pick them out as military from the way they fold their blankets," said one aid worker.

Analysts say that if military elements among the refugees are not disarmed completely, they will be able to sell their arms to Congolese militia, contributing to tension in the runup to the presidential elections at the end of July.
Kintele and Bilolo could together house up to 50,000 refugees, aid organisations said.
